description:
Somos Horum Labs, un equipo de 3 desarrolladores full stack con experiencia en Python, TypeScript y datos. Vamos a trabajar el reto de armonizar los focos de calor de MODIS y VIIRS en un calendario de quemas para Colombia. 
Nuestra pagina: https://www.horumlabs.com/
summary:
Colombia Burn Calendar turns NASA's satellite fire detections into one consistent daily record for any place in Colombia. The challenge is that MODIS and VIIRS count hot spots differently: VIIRS sees much smaller fires (375 m), so merging the two naively makes the VIIRS years look like a sudden jump in burning. We harmonized both sensors into a single series from 1 January 2003 to 13 November 2026. MODIS years are rescaled to VIIRS units with a factor per month, adjusted to each department, and they are clearly marked as estimates.

On top of that we built a web calendar where anyone can pick a department or municipality, or draw their own area, and see whether the current month is normal compared with the history of that same month. It matters because fire seasons in Colombia change a lot from year to year, and the people who plan for them need numbers they can trust, with the limits shown. The method is open, the pipeline is reproducible, and every chart can be downloaded as CSV.
details:
What it does. You open the app, search for a department or municipality (or draw a polygon), and get a daily calendar of hot spots for that area from 2003 to today. Each month is compared with the historical median of the same month and gets an alert level, so unusual activity stands out at a glance. A seasonality matrix shows which months and years burned the most. A History tab, a satellite image of the selected day (NASA GIBS) and CSV downloads (hot spots, daily series, monthly comparison) are there for people who want to check our work.

How the harmonization works. We use FIRMS hot spots from MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), apply quality filters, and take VIIRS as the reference sensor. MODIS is converted to VIIRS units with one factor per month, adjusted to each department. Before looking at any result, we set a test with margins (15% national, 30% per department). Where the test did not pass, or could not be run at that scale (municipalities and drawn areas), the app shows a warning instead of hiding the problem. We also compared our numbers with the IDEAM semester reports, only to validate, never as input.

Benefits and impact. Land managers, responders and curious citizens can anticipate critical fire seasons and see whether a year is really unusual or just looks that way because of the sensor change. We made a point of being honest: hot spots are satellite thermal anomalies, not confirmed fires, and the 2003–2011 values are estimates.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, DuckDB, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj) for the data pipeline; React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and Turf.js for the web app; NASA FIRMS and GIBS as data; DANE boundaries for 1,122 municipality-level areas; CARTO/OpenStreetMap for the basemap. Accessibility is checked with an automated script.

What makes it different. Most fire maps show points. We built a calendar that answers "is this normal?" and shows its own uncertainty. Everything runs from the raw files with scripts in the repository, so anyone can reproduce it.

Team and AI. The method and every decision were ours: filters, reference sensor, seasonal baseline, alert levels, test margins. We used AI to speed up the work: Claude Code wrote most of the code and documentation, and Claude Desktop helped with sources and descriptive tables. The demo video was produced with Claude Code, and its narration was generated with ElevenLabs using the voice of one of our team members. No AI-generated images are used, and no NASA logos or emblems appear anywhere.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS active fire data)
